title: Machine Learning for Phishing Detection: A Systematic Review and Cross-Dataset Evaluation
abstract: Phishing detection systems increasingly rely on machine learning (ML) classifiers trained on lexical and structural features of URLs and webpage content. However, these models frequently suffer severe performance degradation when deployed across disparate datasets. In this systematic review, we comprehensively evaluate 14 machine learning algorithms across four benchmark datasets (PhishTank, OpenPhish, Alexa, and Common Crawl). We show that while models achieve over 98% accuracy in intra-dataset evaluation, cross-dataset transfer reduces accuracy by up to 34% due to feature distribution drift and varying class imbalance ratios.

title: On the Robustness of Machine Learning-Based Phishing Detectors Against Evasion Attacks
abstract: Machine learning has emerged as a dominant defense against sophisticated phishing campaigns. Nevertheless, adversarial perturbations designed to preserve visual authenticity while modifying lexical tokens pose a critical threat to classifier reliability. We investigate the robustness of state-of-the-art URL classification models against black-box and gray-box evasion attacks. Our findings demonstrate that slight lexical manipulations such as subdomain homoglyphs and path padding bypass over 72% of decision tree ensembles without altering human user perception.

title: Concept Drift and Aging Effects in Phishing URL Classification
source: Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium
abstract: Security classifiers trained on static distributions inevitably degrade over time as attackers evolve infrastructure and tactics. We examine the temporal degradation of phishing URL classifiers across a longitudinal 3-year collection of over 1.2 million URLs. Using the TESSERACT evaluation framework, we quantify spatial and temporal bias, revealing that standard cross-validation severely overestimates classifier longevity. We propose continuous active learning strategies and temporal confidence re-weighting to mitigate concept drift in production pipelines.

title: PhishLim: A Transformer-Based Approach for Cross-Domain Phishing Webpage Detection
abstract: Existing phishing webpage detectors often rely heavily on domain-specific lexical patterns that fail to generalize across industry verticals (e.g., banking versus cloud services). We introduce PhishLim, a hierarchical Transformer model combining DOM-tree structural embeddings with pre-trained language representations of text content. Across cross-domain experiments comprising 45,000 active websites, PhishLim improves generalization F1-score by 18.4% relative to baseline Random Forest models without requiring target domain retuning.

title: Adversarial Machine Learning in Phishing URL Detection: A Survey
abstract: This survey analyzes the arms race between adversarial attacks and robust defenses in automated phishing URL detection. We categorize adversarial generation techniques into token substitution, homograph manipulation, and benign feature injection. We systematically evaluate defense mechanisms including adversarial training, defensive distillation, and ensemble bagging. Our analysis highlights that while adversarial training provides local robustness, it often degrades nominal accuracy on standard benign traffic distributions.

title: DeepPhish: Simulating Malicious AI for Evading Phishing Detectors
source: ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security (AISEC)
abstract: Attackers can leverage generative deep learning algorithms to synthesize synthetic phishing URLs that bypass contemporary machine learning detectors. We propose DeepPhish, a generative recurrent neural network architecture trained on malicious URL syntax to output highly realistic yet evasive URLs. In extensive empirical tests against Google Safe Browsing and commercial neural detectors, DeepPhish generated URLs achieved a bypass rate exceeding 80% while retaining functional web redirections.

title: Catching the Phish: Evaluating Feature Decay and Model Drift in Real-Time Phishing Scanners
source: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
abstract: Real-time automated phishing detection is challenged by agile adversary tactics, fast-flux DNS configurations, and disposable domains. Tracking 180,000 live phishing campaigns over 12 months, we demonstrate that traditional hand-crafted lexical features suffer steep decay within 14 days of model deployment. We propose a resilient multi-modal architecture that pairs dynamic DOM rendering with cryptographic certificate metadata, maintaining 94% true positive rates over extended deployment windows.

title: Generalization Bounds for Machine Learning Classifiers in Adversarial Phishing Environments
source: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
abstract: We develop theoretical generalization bounds for empirical risk minimization classifiers operating under adversarial covariate shift in phishing identification. By formulating attacker cost functions as optimal transport metrics, we prove that classifiers optimizing strictly for empirical empirical risk incur unbounded worst-case generalization error under bounded domain perturbations. We introduce an invariant risk minimization objective that bounds transfer error across multi-institution security telemetries.

title: A Comparative Study of Deep Learning and Classical ML for Phishing URL Detection
source: Journal of Network and Computer Applications
abstract: We present an extensive empirical comparison between classical machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines) and deep neural architectures (CNN, LSTM, Transformer) for phishing URL detection. Using a standardized corpus of 500,000 URLs, we evaluate raw character-level embeddings versus expert-engineered manual features. While deep neural networks excel at extracting implicit syntactic patterns, classical models with robust feature selection prove significantly faster and more resilient to out-of-distribution noise.

title: PhishBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark Dataset and Evaluation Framework for Web Phishing
source: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
abstract: Existing phishing benchmarks suffer from severe class imbalance, lack of temporal split validations, and absence of full webpage artifacts. We present PhishBench, an open-access multimodal benchmark comprising 250,000 validated phishing instances paired with DOM snapshots, screenshots, network traffic captures, and SSL certificate chains. We benchmark 12 leading commercial and open-source models, establishing baseline cross-dataset generalization metrics across internationalized domains and brand impersonations.

title: Visual Phishing Detection: A Review of Computer Vision and Deep Learning Approaches
abstract: Visual similarity attacks circumvent text-based phishing filters by rendering critical brand assets via canvas elements, CSS transformations, and SVG overlays. This survey examines visual phishing detection frameworks employing computer vision algorithms, including SIFT feature matching, OCR text alignment, and Siamese deep neural networks. We assess detection latency, false alarm rates on responsive web templates, and resilience against adversarial visual perturbations such as alpha blending and perspective tilting.

title: Robust Phishing Detection via Multi-Modal Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Single-modality phishing detection is vulnerable when attackers intentionally omit or obfuscate individual channels (e.g. shortening URLs or omitting webpage text). We design MMGNN, a multi-modal graph neural network that models the heterogeneous interactions among URL lexical tokens, DOM tree structures, and external WHOIS/DNS metadata. Across three benchmark datasets, MMGNN exhibits superior cross-dataset transferability, outperforming single-modal baselines by 12.3% in AUC-ROC when facing cross-domain zero-day campaigns.

title: Mitigating Bias and Dataset Drift in Automated Phishing Classification Pipelines
source: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
abstract: Phishing detection algorithms trained on public feeds such as PhishTank and OpenPhish inherit strong reporting biases, leading models to memorize specific target brands or high-frequency registrar names rather than learning general malicious behaviors. We examine the impact of sampling bias on model generalization and demonstrate that debiasing via sample reweighting and domain-adversarial training reduces false positive rates on benign corporate intranets from 4.7% down to 0.12%.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Phishing Website Detection
abstract: Black-box machine learning classifiers in cybersecurity hinder incident response teams from understanding detection rationales and diagnosing false alarms. We integrate SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME into tree ensemble and neural network phishing detectors. Our empirical findings show that explanation fidelity allows security analysts to detect shortcut learning—such as reliance on ephemeral TLD features—and significantly improves trust and operator triage speed.

title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning for Zero-Day Phishing URL Detection
source: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing
abstract: Label scarcity in real-time security operations prevents supervised models from reacting swiftly to novel zero-day phishing variants. We propose PhishSSL, a contrastive self-supervised pre-training method on unlabelled URL corpora that learns invariant semantic and topological character distributions. Fine-tuning on only 1% labelled target instances matches fully supervised baselines and increases cross-dataset out-of-distribution F1-score from 74.2% to 89.6%.

title: Analyzing the Impact of Adversarial Perturbations on Deep Learning Phishing Classifiers
abstract: We analyze the sensitivity of convolutional and recurrent neural network phishing classifiers to character insertions, deletions, and Unicode zero-width sequences. Through targeted gradient-based perturbations, we discover that minimal URL transformations causing less than 2% edit distance drop model detection rates from 97% to under 15%. We discuss practical defenses, including text normalization layers, character token pooling, and adversarial data augmentation.

title: Cross-Dataset Robustness Evaluation of Machine Learning for Malicious URL Identification
source: IEEE Conference on Dependable and Secure Computing
abstract: Machine learning papers in malicious URL detection often claim near-perfect accuracies on isolated datasets. In this study, we cross-evaluate six widely cited models across four heterogeneous public datasets (ISCX-URL2016, PhishTank, Ebbu2017, and Alexa). We observe that model accuracy drops by 20% to 45% under cross-dataset testing. We identify key factors driving the performance collapse: inconsistent ground-truth labelling criteria, differing class imbalance, and distinct temporal windows.

title: PhishTrans: Transformer-Based Cross-Language Phishing Detection with Contextual Embeddings
abstract: Multilingual phishing campaigns exploit localized idioms and non-Latin character sets to evade monolingual English classifiers. We formulate PhishTrans, utilizing multilingual BERT embeddings fine-tuned on bilingual and trilingual phishing emails and landing pages. In cross-lingual experiments covering English, Spanish, and Arabic phishing attacks, PhishTrans maintains a balanced F1 score of 93.1%, proving robust against language-switching evasions.

title: Evaluation of Machine Learning Classifiers for Phishing Webpage Detection Under Concept Drift
abstract: Phishing detection is an ongoing game where scammers update their webpage source code and hosting techniques. We evaluate seven classification algorithms over time-stamped datasets collected between 2015 and 2018. Decision trees and Random Forests demonstrate higher initial accuracy but degrade precipitously over six months compared to deep learning models with natural language processing features. We propose scheduled retraining strategies to maintain defensive resilience.

title: A Longitudinal Study of Phishing Infrastructure and Machine Learning Detection Longevity
source: ACM Transactions on Privacy and Security (TOPS)
abstract: How long do machine learning models remain effective without model updates? We analyze 2.4 million phishing encounters gathered over four years from a tier-1 threat intelligence provider. We show that lexical URL classifiers lose 50% of their discriminative power within 90 days as phishing kits migrate to new cloud providers (e.g. Firebase, IPFS). In contrast, structural DOM layout and visual brand identity features demonstrate significantly longer shelf life.

title: Robustness of Deep Learning Models for Malicious URL Detection Under Black-Box Attacks
abstract: Evaluating black-box evasion robustness is critical for deploying deep neural classifiers in hostile cyber environments. We propose a mutation-based attack harness that generates functionally equivalent URLs using benign sub-string concatenation, redirection chains, and IP obfuscation. Our results reveal that deep CNN and RNN architectures are significantly more fragile than previously recognized, experiencing a 60% drop in true positive rates under minimal string mutation budgets.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning for Phishing Detection: Real-World Datasets and Reproducibility
abstract: Reproducibility in phishing detection research is impeded by transient URLs, dead websites, and unstandardized data splitting. In this benchmark study, we aggregate and re-validate 100,000 active phishing and benign websites, providing full DOM trees, HTTP headers, and URL tokens. We demonstrate that random k-fold cross-validation inflates F1 scores by up to 22% compared to time-aware splitting, highlighting the imperative for standardized benchmark protocols.

title: Adversarial Robustness in Phishing Detection: A Comprehensive Taxonomy and Defense Framework
abstract: Adversarial machine learning presents an acute challenge for automated cyber defenses. In this paper, we structure a taxonomy of 23 distinct adversarial attacks on phishing classifiers, categorized by adversary capability (white-box, gray-box, black-box) and attack phase (poisoning vs evasion). We propose a defense framework incorporating certified robust training and input sanitization, yielding provable lower bounds on accuracy degradation under worst-case bounded perturbations.

title: Cross-Dataset Validation of Feature Sets for Phishing Webpage Classification
abstract: Feature engineering determines both nominal accuracy and generalization resilience in phishing detection. We evaluate 58 features spanning URL lexical statistics, page content keywords, external reputation APIs, and SSL parameters across three open benchmark datasets. We identify a robust subset of 14 invariant features that achieves 96.2% cross-dataset accuracy, whereas full feature vectors collapse to 68.4% due to severe overfitting on dataset-specific noise.

title: Domain Adaptation and Transfer Learning for Robust Phishing Detection Across Emerging Threats
source: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
abstract: When cyber criminals pivot to new attack tactics (such as QR-code phishing or web3 impersonation), supervised models trained on legacy campaigns fail. We propose a transfer learning framework utilizing Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) adversarial domain alignment. By aligning deep latent feature representations between legacy phishing datasets and unlabelled live traffic, our model recovers 91.5% classification accuracy on previously unseen emerging phishing campaigns.
